title: NEC Articles 300–398 — Wiring Methods & Materials
description: Installation requirements for conduit, cables, raceways, and conductors per NEC 2023 Articles 300–398. 30 questions.

questions.question: The NEC requires all conductors of the same circuit to be in the same raceway, cable, or trench. What is the primary reason for this requirement?
choices: To reduce voltage drop across long circuit runs
To prevent inductive heating of ferrous metal raceways and enclosures
To allow easier identification of circuit conductors during maintenance
To meet the minimum fill requirements of Table 1, Chapter 9
questions.answer: To prevent inductive heating of ferrous metal raceways and enclosures
questions.explanation: NEC 300.3(B) requires all conductors of the same circuit — including the neutral and equipment grounding conductor — to be grouped together in the same raceway, cable, or trench. When AC current flows through conductors, each conductor produces a magnetic field. If conductors of the same circuit are separated into different ferrous metal (steel) raceways, the alternating magnetic fields cannot cancel each other, causing inductive heating of the raceway, increased impedance, and potentially overheated conduit and enclosures.

questions.question: When a cable is installed through a wood framing member and is within 1¼ inches of the nearest edge, what protection is required?
choices: A plastic bushing listed for the purpose
A steel nail plate at least 1/16 inch thick covering the area of the wiring
A minimum of ½-inch conduit sleeve through the framing member
No protection is required if the cable is rated at 600V
questions.answer: A steel nail plate at least 1/16 inch thick covering the area of the wiring
questions.explanation: NEC 300.4(A)(1) requires that where a cable is installed through bored holes in wood framing members and those holes are within 1¼ inches of the nearest edge of the framing member, a steel plate or bushing at least 1/16 inch thick shall be installed to protect the cable from nails or screws driven through the finished surface. This prevents fasteners during drywall installation or finishing work from penetrating the cable and causing a fault.

questions.question: Which wiring method requires the shallowest minimum cover depth when buried underground?
choices: Direct burial cables rated for the purpose — 24 inches
PVC conduit (Schedule 80) — 18 inches
Rigid metal conduit (RMC) or intermediate metal conduit (IMC) — 6 inches
Rigid nonmetallic conduit (Schedule 40 PVC) — 12 inches
questions.answer: Rigid metal conduit (RMC) or intermediate metal conduit (IMC) — 6 inches
questions.explanation: NEC Table 300.5 specifies minimum cover requirements for underground wiring. Rigid metal conduit (RMC) and intermediate metal conduit (IMC) require the least depth — only 6 inches of cover — because their rigid metal construction provides the greatest physical protection. Direct burial cables require 24 inches, nonmetallic conduit (Schedule 40) requires 18 inches under most conditions, and 12 inches applies under certain conditions with concrete encasement.

questions.question: The NEC requires that wiring within a ceiling assembly be supported independently of the ceiling infrastructure. Which of the following would violate this requirement?
choices: A conduit supported by a trapeze hanger attached to the building structure
A cable supported by its own J-hooks attached to the building structure
A raceway using the ceiling grid T-bar or hanger wires as support
A conduit supported from unistrut attached to concrete deck
questions.answer: A raceway using the ceiling grid T-bar or hanger wires as support
questions.explanation: NEC 300.11(A) requires that wiring methods be secured and supported independently of a suspended ceiling and may not use the ceiling grid support wires as support. Suspended ceiling grids and their hanger wires are not designed for electrical load and can be displaced during seismic events or ceiling modifications. Wiring must be supported directly from the building structure using its own hangers, J-hooks, trapeze hangers, or other approved means.

questions.question: The NEC requires free conductors at outlets and switch points. What is the minimum free length of conductor that must be left at each outlet, junction, or switch point for splicing or connection to a device?
choices: 3 inches total, with at least 1 inch extending beyond the box opening
6 inches measured from the point where it emerges from the raceway or cable sheath, with at least 3 inches extending past the front opening of the box
8 inches total, measured from the back of the box
4 inches total free conductor with no minimum extension requirement
questions.answer: 6 inches measured from the point where it emerges from the raceway or cable sheath, with at least 3 inches extending past the front opening of the box
questions.explanation: NEC 300.14 requires a minimum of 6 inches of free conductor at each outlet, junction, and switch point for splices or connection to devices. Additionally, where a conductor is less than 6 inches in length and the box opening is less than 8 inches in any direction, the conductors must extend at least 3 inches outside the front opening of the box. This ensures sufficient conductor length for safe splicing and device connections without straining the termination.

questions.question: The number and size of conductors in a raceway shall be not more than will permit dissipation of heat and ready installation or withdrawal of conductors. What documents govern raceway fill?
choices: NFPA 70E Table 130.7 and the equipment manufacturer's specifications
The fill tables in Chapter 9 of the NEC, including Table 1 (percent fill) and associated conduit and conductor area tables
ANSI/UL standards for the specific wiring method only
Local jurisdictional amendments and manufacturer installation instructions
questions.answer: The fill tables in Chapter 9 of the NEC, including Table 1 (percent fill) and associated conduit and conductor area tables
questions.explanation: NEC 300.17 limits conduit and raceway fill, and directs the installer to the fill tables in Chapter 9 of the NEC. Table 1 specifies maximum fill percentages (53% for one conductor, 31% for two conductors, 40% for three or more conductors in most raceways), while Tables 4 through 9 provide the internal dimensions of raceways and the cross-sectional areas of conductors, enabling fill calculations.

questions.question: When calculating conductor ampacity, both a temperature correction factor and a conductor adjustment factor apply simultaneously. How are these two factors applied?
choices: Use whichever factor is more restrictive; do not apply both simultaneously
Add the two factors together and subtract from 100% to get the final derating
Multiply the conductor's base ampacity by both factors applied together (multiply them together)
Apply the temperature correction factor first to get a new base ampacity, then use that value for fill adjustment only if required by the AHJ
questions.answer: Multiply the conductor's base ampacity by both factors applied together (multiply them together)
questions.explanation: Per NEC 310.15, when both ambient temperature correction (for temperatures above the conductor's rated ambient) and conductor adjustment factors (for more than three current-carrying conductors) apply, both factors must be applied simultaneously — that is, multiplied together. The corrected ampacity equals the base ampacity multiplied by the temperature correction factor multiplied by the adjustment factor. Using only one or selecting the more restrictive of the two is not correct NEC application.

questions.question: What is required for cables entering cabinets and cutout boxes?
choices: Cables shall enter only through the bottom of the cabinet to prevent moisture entry
Cables shall be secured to the cabinet or cutout box
Cables shall maintain a minimum bending radius of 5× the cable diameter at the cabinet entry
Cables entering metal cabinets must use insulated bushings at each entry point
questions.answer: Cables shall be secured to the cabinet or cutout box
questions.explanation: NEC 312.5(C) requires that cables entering a cabinet or cutout box be secured to the cabinet. This prevents the cable from being pulled out of the enclosure due to tension on the cable run, which could loosen terminations and create a shock or arc hazard. Cable clamps, connectors, or other fittings listed for the purpose are used to secure cables at their point of entry.

questions.question: For a straight pull through a pull box,the length of the box is required to be at least how many times the trade size of the largest raceway entering the box?
choices: 6 times the trade size of the largest raceway
8 times the trade size of the largest raceway
10 times the trade size of the largest raceway
12 times the trade size of the largest raceway
questions.answer: 8 times the trade size of the largest raceway
questions.explanation: NEC 314.28(A)(1) requires that for a straight pull, the minimum length of a pull box or junction box shall be not less than 8 times the trade size diameter of the largest raceway. This dimension ensures that conductors can be pulled through without excessive bending or stress on conductor insulation. For example, a straight pull with a 3-inch raceway requires a box at least 24 inches (8 × 3) long in the direction of the pull.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes where rigid metal conduit (RMC) RMC is permitted?
choices: RMC is permitted only in dry and damp locations, not in wet or corrosive environments
RMC is permitted in all atmospheric conditions and all occupancies, and is suitable for direct burial and concrete encasement
RMC is permitted in commercial and industrial occupancies only
RMC is permitted only where subject to physical damage
questions.answer: RMC is permitted in all atmospheric conditions and all occupancies, and is suitable for direct burial and concrete encasement
questions.explanation: NEC 344.10 states that rigid metal conduit (RMC) shall be permitted under all atmospheric conditions and occupancies, including direct burial in the earth and embedment in concrete. RMC is the most universally permitted wiring method in the NEC and is suitable for wet, damp, dry, corrosive, and hazardous locations. Its heavy steel wall construction provides superior mechanical protection compared to other conduit types.

questions.question: Which of the following is a prohibited application for flexible metal conduit (FMC)?
choices: As a wiring method in lengths exceeding 10 feet indoors
In wet locations
In concrete slabs on grade
In commercial cooking equipment connections
questions.answer: In wet locations
questions.explanation: NEC 348.12 prohibits the use of flexible metal conduit (FMC) in wet locations. The interlocking armor of FMC is not a watertight assembly — moisture can penetrate between the spiral armor windings and damage conductor insulation, create corrosion, and cause ground faults. Where flexibility is required in wet locations, liquidtight flexible metal conduit (LFMC) listed for wet locations must be used instead.

questions.question: PVC conduit (rigid nonmetallic conduit) is not permitted in which application?
choices: In wet locations or underground
Where exposed to physical damage, unless the conduit is identified for such use
In buildings of Type I or Type II construction
In hazardous locations of any class or division
questions.answer: Where exposed to physical damage, unless the conduit is identified for such use
questions.explanation: NEC 352.12(A) prohibits the use of PVC conduit (rigid nonmetallic conduit, Schedule 40 or 80) where exposed to physical damage, unless it is identified (listed and labeled) for use in such locations. Standard PVC conduit can crack or shatter when struck, unlike rigid metal conduit. Schedule 80 PVC has thicker walls and may be listed for areas of physical damage in some applications, but the default standard-wall PVC conduit is not permitted in exposed locations subject to damage.

questions.question: <ScrollWheelDown>Which condition makes electrical metallic tubing (EMT) EMT prohibited?
choices: In concrete that is in direct contact with the earth
Where subject to severe physical damage
In dry commercial locations
Where the conduit is longer than 100 feet without a pull point
questions.answer: Where subject to severe physical damage
questions.explanation: NEC 358.12(1) prohibits the use of EMT where it is subject to severe physical damage. EMT has a relatively thin wall compared to rigid metal conduit (RMC) or intermediate metal conduit (IMC), making it vulnerable to crushing, deformation, and penetration from heavy impacts. In areas where severe physical damage is possible — such as near loading docks, in vehicle traffic areas, or in heavily industrial environments — RMC or IMC must be used instead.

questions.question: What restriction applies to using electrical nonmetallic tubing (ENT) in multi-story buildings?
choices: ENT may not be used in any building more than two stories in height
ENT in buildings over three floors must be concealed within walls, floors, or ceilings that provide at least a 15-minute thermal barrier (such as ½-inch gypsum wallboard)
ENT must be encased in concrete in buildings over three stories
ENT requires conduit supports every 2 feet in buildings exceeding three stories
questions.answer: ENT in buildings over three floors must be concealed within walls, floors, or ceilings that provide at least a 15-minute thermal barrier (such as ½-inch gypsum wallboard)
questions.explanation: NEC 362.10 permits ENT in buildings of any height when it is concealed in walls, floors, or ceilings providing a thermal barrier with a minimum 15-minute finish rating (such as ½-inch gypsum wallboard). However, ENT may only be used in exposed applications in buildings of three stories or fewer. This restriction exists because ENT is a combustible nonmetallic material that, if exposed in a multi-story fire, could contribute to fire spread — the 15-minute finish rating provides time for evacuation and fire control.

questions.question: What is the maximum percentage of cross-sectional fill permitted in a metal wireway, and what additional rule applies when there are more than 30 current-carrying conductors?
choices: 40% fill maximum; no adjustment factor required for any number of conductors
20% fill maximum; when more than 30 current-carrying conductors are bundled in any cross section, conductor ampacity adjustment factors of 310.15(C)(1) apply
30% fill maximum; ampacity reduction of 50% required for any wireway installation
25% fill maximum; conductors must be rearranged to equalize temperature rise
questions.answer: 20% fill maximum; when more than 30 current-carrying conductors are bundled in any cross section, conductor ampacity adjustment factors of 310.15(C)(1) apply
questions.explanation: NEC 376.22(A) limits the sum of the cross-sectional areas of all conductors at any cross section of a metal wireway to 20% of the interior cross-sectional area of the wireway. NEC 376.22(B) further requires that where more than 30 current-carrying conductors are installed in any cross section of a wireway, the ampacity of each conductor shall be reduced per the adjustment factors in NEC 310.15(C)(1). Splices and taps within the wireway also count toward the 20% fill rule.

questions.question: What protection is required for cables installed in notches cut into wooden framing members?
choices: The notch must be filled with fire-rated caulking after cable installation
A steel plate at least 1/16 inch thick must be installed over the notch to protect the cable from fasteners
The cable must be enclosed in conduit through the entire length of the notch
No additional protection is required if the notch is in the center of the framing member
questions.answer: A steel plate at least 1/16 inch thick must be installed over the notch to protect the cable from fasteners
questions.explanation: NEC 300.4(B) requires that where cables pass through notches in framing members, the cable shall be protected against physical damage from fasteners (nails and screws) by a steel plate, sleeve, or equivalent protection at least 1/16 inch thick. Notches create a path where a finish nail driven through drywall could easily penetrate the cable. The steel plate provides a hard stop that prevents fastener penetration.

questions.question: What is required when cables or raceways pass through holes or slots in metal framing members (such as metal studs)?
choices: The metal framing member must be grounded to the cable or raceway
Listed bushings or listed grommets must be installed to protect the cables or raceways from the sharp metal edges
The hole diameter must be at least twice the outside diameter of the cable
The cable must be sheathed in liquidtight flexible conduit through the metal framing member
questions.answer: Listed bushings or listed grommets must be installed to protect the cables or raceways from the sharp metal edges
questions.explanation: NEC 300.4(G) requires that where cables or raceways pass through holes in metal framing members (such as metal wall studs), listed bushings or grommets shall be installed to protect the wiring from the sharp edges of the metal. Metal framing members typically have factory-punched knockout holes with edges that can abrade or cut through cable insulation under vibration or movement, potentially causing a ground fault or short circuit.

questions.question: How far above grade must protection be provided for conductors emerging from a direct-buried installation?
choices: From grade level to a minimum of 4 feet above finished grade
From grade level to a minimum of 8 feet above finished grade, or to the point of termination in an enclosure
From grade level to a minimum of 6 feet, with a raceway cover over the exposed portion
No additional protection is needed if the conductor is rated for direct burial
questions.answer: From grade level to a minimum of 8 feet above finished grade, or to the point of termination in an enclosure
questions.explanation: NEC 300.5(D) requires that conductors emerging from underground installations and entering buildings or structures, or rising above grade, be protected by an enclosure or raceway from the point they leave the underground installation to a minimum of 8 feet above finished grade, or to the point of termination where damage is not likely. This protects the conductors from physical damage by lawn equipment, vehicles, or other external forces.

questions.question: Which of the following is a required method for identifying underground conductors at their point of termination?
choices: Conductors must be color-coded red for 240V and black for 120V
Underground conductors must be identified by tagging, marking tape, or other effective means at their terminals
Permanent circuit directories must be posted at all underground pull boxes
Underground conductors must use conductor material (copper vs. aluminum) identification at all splice points
questions.answer: Underground conductors must be identified by tagging, marking tape, or other effective means at their terminals
questions.explanation: NEC 300.5(I) requires that underground conductors be identified by tagging, circuit marking, or other effective means at terminal locations. Because underground conductors may run long distances and connect to equipment remotely, identification at termination points is essential for safe maintenance — workers must be able to verify which conductors belong to which circuit before de-energizing or working on them.

questions.question: NEC 300.7(A) requires that. What is the primary purpose of raceways being sealed where they pass from areas of different temperatures?
choices: To prevent fire from spreading through raceways between temperature zones
To prevent circulation of air through the raceway that could cause condensation to form and travel to equipment
To maintain the temperature rating of conductors passing between zones
To prevent rodents from traveling through raceways between areas
questions.answer: To prevent circulation of air through the raceway that could cause condensation to form and travel to equipment
questions.explanation: NEC 300.7(A) requires raceways to be sealed where they pass between areas of substantially different temperatures (such as from an unheated exterior to a heated interior, or from a refrigerated space). Without sealing, warmer, moisture-laden air traveling through the raceway from the warm side will condense when it encounters cooler temperatures on the other side, depositing moisture in equipment, enclosures, and switchgear where it can cause corrosion, tracking, and ground faults.

questions.question: What is required for metal raceways and enclosures?
choices: Metal raceways must be bonded to the grounded (neutral) conductor at each junction
Metal raceways, cable armor, and other metal enclosures shall be metallically continuous, forming a low-impedance fault current path
Metal raceways must be painted or coated to prevent corrosion and maintain conductivity
Metal raceways must be grounded to earth at intervals not exceeding 100 feet
questions.answer: Metal raceways, cable armor, and other metal enclosures shall be metallically continuous, forming a low-impedance fault current path
questions.explanation: NEC 300.10 requires that metal raceways, cable armor, and metal enclosures form a metallically continuous path. This electrical continuity is essential for the equipment grounding system — it provides the low-impedance fault current return path required to operate overcurrent devices quickly when a ground fault occurs. Poor connections between raceway sections can create high-impedance paths that allow dangerous touch voltages to persist even when a fault exists.

questions.question: What is required for mechanical continuity of raceways?
choices: Metal raceways must be supported at intervals not exceeding 3 feet to ensure mechanical continuity
Raceways and cable sheaths shall be continuous between outlets, boxes, devices, and fittings — they must not be intermittent
Raceways must be installed in one continuous length without couplings between any two junction boxes
Mechanical continuity requires that all conduit runs be installed with expansion fittings every 50 feet
questions.answer: Raceways and cable sheaths shall be continuous between outlets, boxes, devices, and fittings — they must not be intermittent
questions.explanation: NEC 300.12 requires that raceways and cable sheaths be continuous — that is, mechanically intact from outlet to outlet, from outlet to box, or between fitting and fitting, without gaps or breaks. This requirement ensures that conductors are continuously enclosed and protected, that the equipment grounding path is maintained, and that fire stops and other building integrity features remain intact throughout the raceway system.

questions.question: The NEC requires a box or conduit body wherever conductors are spliced or where a device is installed. Which of the following situations would require a listed box or conduit body?
choices: A continuous conductor passing through a pull fitting with no splice
A splice in a conductor inside a length of conduit without a box
A conductor entering a listed lighting fixture through a listed conduit nipple
A continuous run of MC cable between two panels without taps
questions.answer: A splice in a conductor inside a length of conduit without a box
questions.explanation: NEC 300.15 requires that a box or conduit body be installed at every point where conductors are spliced, where a device is installed, where a luminaire or other equipment is connected, or where conductors are accessed. A splice inside a conduit without a box is a clear violation — all splices must be in listed boxes or conduit bodies that provide accessible, enclosed, and protected splice points to allow future inspection and maintenance.

questions.question: If a single ungrounded conductor must be installed in a ferrous metal raceway, what must be done to prevent inductive heating?
choices: The conduit must be bonded to ground at both ends to dissipate induced currents
All conductors of the circuit — including the neutral and equipment grounding conductor — must be installed in the same ferrous metal raceway
The conductor must be derated by 50% to account for induced heating losses
The raceway must be aluminum or nonmetallic to prevent inductive effects
questions.answer: All conductors of the circuit — including the neutral and equipment grounding conductor — must be installed in the same ferrous metal raceway
questions.explanation: NEC 300.20 requires that where single conductors carrying alternating current are installed in ferrous metal (iron or steel) raceways, all conductors of that circuit must be in the same raceway. A single conductor in a ferrous metal conduit creates a magnetic circuit through the conduit that cannot cancel, causing inductive heating of the conduit. With all conductors of the circuit together, their magnetic fields cancel each other and heating is prevented. This parallels the requirement in 300.3(B).

questions.question: If a conductor is rated for 75°C and is installed where the ambient temperature is 50°C (instead of the standard 30°C reference), how does the correction factor affect the conductor ampacity?
choices: The ampacity is increased because the insulation is rated higher than the ambient
The ampacity is reduced by multiplying by a correction factor less than 1.0, because the elevated ambient reduces the conductor's ability to dissipate heat
No correction is required until ambient temperature exceeds the conductor's insulation rating
The ampacity is reduced by a flat 25% regardless of insulation temperature rating
questions.answer: The ampacity is reduced by multiplying by a correction factor less than 1.0, because the elevated ambient reduces the conductor's ability to dissipate heat
questions.explanation: NEC 310.15(B) provides ambient temperature correction factors that are applied when the ambient temperature differs from the 30°C (86°F) reference temperature used in the ampacity tables. When ambient temperature exceeds 30°C, the conductor's ability to dissipate heat is reduced, so the allowable current (ampacity) is reduced by multiplying by a correction factor less than 1.0. The higher the ambient temperature relative to the conductor's insulation rating, the smaller the correction factor and the greater the derating.

questions.question: When more than 3 current-carrying conductors are bundled together or installed in a single conduit, adjustment factors are required. What adjustment factor applies when there are 7 to 9 current-carrying conductors?
choices: 80% of the base ampacity
70% of the base ampacity
60% of the base ampacity
50% of the base ampacity
questions.answer: 70% of the base ampacity
questions.explanation: NEC 310.15(C)(1) provides conductor adjustment factors (formerly in Table 310.15(C)(1)) for when more than 3 current-carrying conductors are in a raceway or cable: 4–6 conductors = 80%, 7–9 conductors = 70%, 10–20 conductors = 50%, 21–30 conductors = 45%, 31–40 conductors = 40%, and over 40 conductors = 35%. With 7 to 9 current-carrying conductors, the adjustment factor is 70% — the conductor ampacity from the applicable table is multiplied by 0.70.

questions.question: What is counted as a conductor equivalent when calculating fill for a device box?
choices: Only current-carrying conductors; equipment grounding conductors and cable clamps are exempt from box fill

Each ungrounded and grounded circuit conductor counts as one, all grounding conductors together count as one, each internal cable clamp counts as one, and each yoke-mounted device counts as two conductors
Only the line conductors count; neutral conductors are excluded from box fill
All conductors count as one equivalent regardless of size, plus one additional for the device
questions.answer: Each ungrounded and grounded circuit conductor counts as one, all grounding conductors together count as one, each internal cable clamp counts as one, and each yoke-mounted device counts as two conductors
questions.explanation: NEC 314.16(A) and Table 314.16(B) govern box fill. Each conductor entering the box and terminating or being spliced counts as one conductor equivalent (based on the largest conductor in the box for grounding conductors). All equipment grounding conductors together count as a single conductor. Internal cable clamps count as one conductor equivalent total. Each yoke-mounted device (switch, receptacle) counts as two conductor equivalents. This total, multiplied by the volume per conductor from Table 314.16(B), must not exceed the box's listed volume.

questions.question: For angle pulls or U-pulls through a pull or junction box, the NEC requires a minimum distance. How is this minimum distance calculated for an angle pull?
choices: At least 8 times the trade size of the largest raceway on that wall
At least 6 times the trade size of the largest raceway entering the angle pull, plus the sum of the diameters of all other raceways entering the same wall
At least 10 times the trade size of the largest raceway for an angle pull
At least 4 times the trade size of the largest raceway plus 6 inches for each additional raceway on that wall
questions.answer: At least 6 times the trade size of the largest raceway entering the angle pull, plus the sum of the diameters of all other raceways entering the same wall
questions.explanation: NEC 314.28(A)(2) requires that for angle pulls or U-pulls, the distance from the raceway entry to the opposite wall (or the distance between opposite entry raceways for a U-pull) shall be at least 6 times the trade size of the largest raceway, plus the sum of the trade sizes of any other raceways on the same wall. For example, a box with a 3-inch and a 2-inch conduit on the same wall for an angle pull must be at least (6×3) + 2 = 20 inches in the pull direction.

questions.question: What is the maximum interval between  rigid metal conduit (RMC) supports, and how close to a box or fitting must support be provided?
choices: Every 6 feet; within 2 feet of each box or fitting
Every 10 feet; within 3 feet of each outlet box, junction box, cabinet, or fitting
Every 12 feet; within 4 feet of each box or fitting
Every 8 feet; within 3 feet of each box, fitting, or termination
questions.answer: Every 10 feet; within 3 feet of each outlet box, junction box, cabinet, or fitting
questions.explanation: NEC 344.30 requires that rigid metal conduit (RMC) be securely fastened within 3 feet of each outlet box, junction box, cabinet, conduit body, or other termination point, and at intervals not exceeding 10 feet. This support requirement ensures that the conduit system remains mechanically stable, maintains its routing, and does not sag or shift — all of which are critical for both the mechanical protection of conductors and the integrity of the equipment grounding path.

questions.question: What are the maximum support intervals for electrical metallic tubing (EMT)?
choices: Every 6 feet, and within 2 feet of each box or fitting
Every 10 feet, and within 3 feet of each outlet box, junction box, cabinet, or fitting
Every 8 feet, and within 3 feet of each termination
Every 5 feet, and within 18 inches of each box, device, or fitting
questions.answer: Every 10 feet, and within 3 feet of each outlet box, junction box, cabinet, or fitting
questions.explanation: NEC 358.30 requires EMT to be securely fastened within 3 feet of each outlet box, junction box, device box, cabinet, or other conduit termination, and at intervals not exceeding 10 feet. These same spacing requirements apply to both RMC (344.30) and EMT (358.30), though the specific fastening methods differ. Proper support prevents sagging, vibration-induced loosening at fittings, and maintains the mechanical and electrical integrity of the EMT system.
